newsitem.title: TURKEY: Erdemir sale problems cloud Turkey sell-off plans.
newsitem.headline: Erdemir sale problems cloud Turkey sell-off plans.

text.p: Turkey's privatisation hopes, boosted by a recent court decision allowing the sell-off of its telecom company, are being marred by a lack of interest in the sale of the country's only flat steel producer Erdemir.
In a tender last month only two bids were received for a 30-40 percent stake in Eregli Demir ve Celik Fabrikalari A.S., a profitable concern and consistent good performer.

The government has said it will go ahead with the sale -- its second attempt at the block sale of Erdemir shares since the decision to privatise was taken in 1987 -- despite the lower-than-expected interest.
"This is a disgrace -- the sale is hasty and mishandled," former Erdemir chairman Tevfik Ertuzun told Reuters.
The bidders have not yet met the privatisation board amid speculation the sale may be about to be cancelled again.

"The conditions of the tender were met -- but we are still waiting for an invitation to the negotiations," Tahsin Aldan, chairman of Zonguldak Investment A.S., told Reuters late on Wednesday. His company put in a joint offer with a group of investors. The other bid came from Rumeli Metal Sanayii A.S.

The six-month-old government, which inherited a privatisation programme that has barely moved on for 10 years, was boosted last month after the constitutional court gave the go-ahead for the sale of the state telecoms company.
Partial privatisations of Turk Telekom and Erdemir are among sales Turkey aims to complete in 1997 to the tune of $5 billion.
The Islamist-led government hopes the proceeds will go some way towards clogging Turkey's bulging deficits.
"Turkey really needs a few success stories, and Erdemir is a monopoly and a very attractive company," Erhan Topas, general manager of Gedik Menkul, told Reuters.
"But the offers are not high. I think the tender came too quickly and I don't think it was marketed very well," he said.

Erdemir reported nine month profits of 2.95 trillion lira ($32.3 million) in 1996, down sharply from 8.59 trillion ($175.7 million in the same 1995 period. But the fall was mainly due to high interest payments on $1.5 billion spent on a seven-year programme to increase capacity and modernise.
Net sales rose to 47.3 trillion ($517.5 million) in 1996 from 26.4 trillion lira ($539.9 million).
Ertuzun said the whole company was worth some $6 billion. "But I don't think anyone will pay the kind of money it is worth in the sale. They'll pay half at most," Ertuzun said.

The government holds a 51.66 percent stake in Erdemir and plans to retain a golden share to ensure work continues in the improvement programme, to safeguard foreign debts guaranteed by the treasury and to protect workers' jobs.
The Capital Markets Board introduced a directive last month obliging block buyers in the company to offer the same share price to existing small shareholders.
Bankers say both factors may have reduced demand in the company, but that this does not fully explain the disinterest.

"I can't say I understand why there are just two bids," said a private banker in Istanbul. "But I am less hopeful than during the previous privatisation effort and I am worried that this time also it may be cancelled."
Eight groups -- some including foreign companies -- bid in the first tender last year, which was cancelled in May to allow more time for potential investors to put in bids.
Since then, three rating agencies, including Standard and Poor's, have downgraded Turkey's foreign currency rating and a fourth, Moody's, has put the country on creditwatch.
"Foreigners are probably not interested any more because confidence in Turkey has been shaken," the private banker said.
Ertuzun said Turkish companies, too, appeared fed up with what he called the government's haphazard manner prompted by its desparation to privatise at all costs.

Salomon Brothers has offered to conduct the sale through convertible bonds to bring in more money quickly and defuse the negative effects of the golden share, Western bankers said. They are still awaiting a reply.
Bankers say the sell-off plan would not be dented too much by another failure in Erdemir as long as other concerns, such as refinery Tupras or petroleum marketer Petrol Ofisi, were sold.
But there is much uncertainty over whether or when legislation related to these sales will be passed by parliament.
"There is still good feeling at the moment. But if nothing concrete is done this optimism will suffer," Topas said.
